hello.note: Reply: wa alaikum assalam (وعلیکم السلام). Casual: salam.

goodbye.note: Also very common: Allah hafiz (اللہ حافظ).

please.note: A little formal. In speech: meharbani kar ke (مہربانی کر کے), or simply 'please'.

thank_you.note: Thank you very much: bohat shukriya (بہت شکریہ).

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it's nothing'. The usual reply to thanks.

yes.note: Casual: haan (ہاں). A soft ji (جی) on its own is also a polite yes.

sorry.note: Also common: maazrat (معذرت), or simply the English 'sorry'.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'please listen'. The usual way to get a stranger's attention.

good_morning.note: Many people simply say assalam-o-alaikum at any time of day.

how_are_you.note: To a woman: aap kaisi hain? (آپ کیسی ہیں؟). Either gender: aap ka kya haal hai?

im_fine.note: Very common reply: Alhamdulillah, theek hoon (الحمدللہ، ٹھیک ہوں).

whats_your_name.note: Extra polite: aap ka ism-e-shareef? (آپ کا اسمِ شریف؟)

nice_to_meet_you.text: آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی
nice_to_meet_you.roman: Aap se mil kar khushi hui
nice_to_meet_you.note: Same for men and women: hui agrees with khushi (joy), not with the speaker.

speak_english.note: To a woman: kya aap angrezi bolti hain? (کیا آپ انگریزی بولتی ہیں؟)

dont_understand.note: A woman says: main samjhi nahin (میں سمجھی نہیں).

speak_slowly.note: In everyday speech often just: zara aahista boliye.

what.note: Didn't catch what someone said? A polite ji? (جی؟) is softer.

how_much.note: For a feminine item (e.g. kitaab, book): yeh kitne ki hai? (یہ کتنے کی ہے؟)

where_bathroom.note: Washroom is the usual polite word in Pakistan; bathroom and toilet are understood too.

can_you_help.text: کیا آپ میری مدد کر سکتے ہیں؟
can_you_help.roman: Kya aap meri madad kar sakte hain?
can_you_help.note: To a woman: kya aap meri madad kar sakti hain? (کیا آپ میری مدد کر سکتی ہیں؟)

what_time.note: Also very common: kitne baje hain? (کتنے بجے ہیں؟)

five.note: The n only nasalises the vowel. Urdu digit: ۵

eight.note: The th is a hard t with a puff of air, not English th. Urdu digit: ۸

nine.note: Said like British 'gnaw', not English 'now'. Urdu digit: ۹

coffee.note: Same word as kaafi, 'enough'; context makes it clear.

tea.note: By default this means strong milky tea. Green tea: sabz chaye (سبز چائے).

bread.note: Roti is the everyday flatbread. Sliced loaf bread: dabal roti (ڈبل روٹی).

menu_please.note: De dijiye is a polite 'please give'.

bill_please.note: Literally 'please bring the bill'. Also: bill de dijiye.

delicious.note: A bit more refined: bohat lazeez hai (بہت لذیذ ہے).

no_meat.note: A woman says: main gosht nahin khaati (میں گوشت نہیں کھاتی).

enjoy_meal.note: There is no exact 'bon appétit'; hosts invite guests to begin with this. Formal: khana nosh farmaiye.

left.note: In directions also: ulte haath (الٹے ہاتھ), 'on the left hand'.

right.note: In directions also: seedhe haath (سیدھے ہاتھ), 'on the right hand'. Seedha alone means straight.

straight_ahead.note: Go straight ahead: seedhe chale jaaiye (سیدھے چلے جائیے).

stop_here.note: Drivers are often addressed as bhai (brother): bhai, yahan rok dein.

airport.note: The everyday word. Formal and on some signs: hawai adda (ہوائی اڈہ).

hotel.note: In Pakistan hotel can also mean a small roadside eatery.

want_to_go.note: Same for men and women. Also: main … jaana chahta hoon (a woman: chahti hoon).

is_it_far.note: How far is it? kitni door hai? (کتنی دور ہے؟)

too_expensive.note: For a feminine item: yeh bohat mehngi hai (یہ بہت مہنگی ہے).

cheaper.text: کیا اس سے سستا کچھ ہے؟
cheaper.roman: Kya is se sasta kuch hai?
cheaper.note: In shops people also say: kuch sasta dikhaiye (کچھ سستا دکھائیے), 'show me something cheaper'.

id_like_this.note: Politer, pointing at it: yeh de dijiye (یہ دے دیجیے), 'please give me this'.

just_looking.note: A woman says: main bas dekh rahi hoon (میں بس دیکھ رہی ہوں).

pay_card.text: کیا کارڈ سے ادائیگی ہو سکتی ہے؟
pay_card.roman: Kya card se adaigi ho sakti hai?
pay_card.note: Very common in shops: card chalega? (کارڈ چلے گا؟)

cash.note: In shops people mostly say cash (کیش).

open.note: Most shop signs in Pakistan are in English; this is how you say it.

big.note: With feminine nouns: bari (بڑی). The r is a flapped retroflex sound.

tomorrow.note: Same word as 'yesterday'; the future tense of the verb tells you which.

yesterday.note: Same word as 'tomorrow'; the past tense of the verb tells you which.

now.note: Right now. Ab (اب) is 'now' as in 'from now on'.

good_evening.note: Understood but not often said; most people greet with assalam-o-alaikum.

good_night.note: Said at bedtime. When leaving at night, people usually say Allah hafiz.

see_you_later.note: Usually followed by Allah hafiz or khuda hafiz.

help.note: Literally 'save me!'. For non-urgent help: madad kijiye (مدد کیجیے).

call_police.note: In a real emergency people shout: police ko bulao! Police emergency number in Pakistan: 15.

im_lost.note: A woman says: main raasta bhool gayi hoon (میں راستہ بھول گئی ہوں).

pharmacy.note: The everyday word in Pakistan. Also: pharmacy (فارمیسی).

lost_phone.text: میرا فون گم ہو گیا ہے
lost_phone.roman: Mera phone gum ho gaya hai

be_careful.note: Also: ehtiyaat kijiye (احتیاط کیجیے). 'Take care' when parting: apna khayal rakhiye.

no_problem.note: Also very common: koi baat nahin (کوئی بات نہیں).

of_course.note: Politely: ji zaroor (جی ضرور). Also: bilkul (بالکل), 'absolutely'.

im_tired.note: A woman says: main thak gayi hoon (میں تھک گئی ہوں).

welcome.note: At home, hosts often say: aaiye, tashreef laiye (آئیے، تشریف لائیے).

my_family.note: For your household: mere ghar wale (میرے گھر والے). Many people also say meri family.

mother.note: What you call your own mother. General word: maan (ماں); formal: walida (والدہ).

father.note: What you call your own father. Formal and polite: walid (والد); baap (باپ) can sound blunt.

brother.note: Also a friendly, polite way to address any man, e.g. a driver or shopkeeper.

sister.note: To address a woman politely, people often say baji (باجی) or behen ji (بہن جی).

child.note: A girl: bachchi (بچی). Son: beta (بیٹا); daughter: beti (بیٹی).

friend.note: Same word for a male or female friend. A woman's female friend is also called saheli (سہیلی).

this_is_my_friend.note: For a female friend: yeh meri dost hai (یہ میری دوست ہے). More respectful: yeh mere dost hain.

are_you_married.note: Same for men and women. Also common: kya aap ki shaadi ho gayi hai?

have_children.note: Often asked as: aap ke kitne bachche hain? (آپ کے کتنے بچے ہیں؟), 'how many children do you have?'

thursday.note: From juma + raat: 'the eve of Friday'.

friday.note: A common Friday greeting: Juma mubarak (جمعہ مبارک).

saturday.note: Also means 'week'; context makes it clear.

weekend.note: The English word is the everyday one. Formal: ikhtitaam-e-hafta (اختتامِ ہفتہ).

next_week.note: As in 'I'll go next week'. As a subject ('next week is busy'): agla hafta (اگلا ہفتہ).

eleven.note: Every number up to 100 has its own irregular word. Urdu digits: ۱۱

hundred.note: With prices people often say just sau (سو). Urdu digits: ۱۰۰

thousand.note: A hundred thousand is ek lakh (ایک لاکھ). Urdu digits: ۱۰۰۰

how_old.note: Also: aap kitne saal ke hain? (to a woman: kitne saal ki hain?)

years_old.note: Same for men and women. Also: main … saal ka hoon (a woman: saal ki hoon).

red.note: Also: surkh (سرخ), a little more formal. Neither changes for gender.

green.note: With feminine nouns: hari (ہری). Also: sabz (سبز), which never changes.

yellow.note: With feminine nouns: peeli (پیلی). Also: zard (زرد), which never changes.

black.note: With feminine nouns: kaali (کالی). Also: siyah (سیاہ), which never changes.

what_colour.note: For a feminine item: yeh kis rang ki hai? (یہ کس رنگ کی ہے؟)

this_one.note: For a feminine item: yeh wali (یہ والی).

that_one.note: For a feminine item: woh wali (وہ والی).

its_hot.note: Literally 'there's heat'. Very common: bohat garmi hai! (بہت گرمی ہے!)

its_cold.note: Literally 'there's cold'. Also: thand hai (ٹھنڈ ہے).

its_sunny.note: Dhoop is sunshine. Also simply: dhoop hai (دھوپ ہے).

its_windy.note: Literally 'the wind is blowing'. Strong wind: tez hawa (تیز ہوا).

beautiful_day.note: Also: aaj mausam bara suhana hai (آج موسم بڑا سہانا ہے), 'lovely and pleasant'.

summer.note: Also: garmi ka mausam (گرمی کا موسم). In summer: garmiyon mein.

winter.note: Also: sardi ka mausam (سردی کا موسم). In winter: sardiyon mein.

have_reservation.note: Booking is the usual word. Also: mere naam par booking hai, 'it's booked in my name'.

room.note: At hotel desks the English room (روم) is common too.

wifi_password.text: وائی فائی کا پاس ورڈ کیا ہے؟

check_out_time.note: Also: check-out ka waqt kya hai? (چیک آؤٹ کا وقت کیا ہے؟)

map.note: On a phone people usually just say map (میپ) or location.

bus.note: Spelled and said like bas, 'just / enough'; context tells them apart.

next_train.note: At what time: agli train kitne baje hai? (اگلی ٹرین کتنے بجے ہے؟)

is_this_seat_free.note: Khaali means empty. Pointing at it, just: khaali hai? (خالی ہے؟)

what_do_you_do.note: To a woman: aap kya karti hain? (آپ کیا کرتی ہیں؟)

i_work_in.note: A woman says: kaam karti hoon (کام کرتی ہوں). میں is both main (I) and mein (in).

im_student.note: A woman says: main taliba hoon (میں طالبہ ہوں). Also common: main student hoon.

meeting.note: The everyday word at work. Formal: ijlaas (اجلاس).

day_off.note: Also a holiday or leave. 'It's my day off': aaj meri chhutti hai (آج میری چھٹی ہے).

colleague.note: The usual word at work, same for men and women. Formal Urdu: rafeeq-e-kaar (رفیقِ کار).

good_job.note: Said to someone junior or a child. To a peer or senior: bohat achha kaam kiya! (بہت اچھا کام کیا!)

table_for_two.text: دو لوگوں کے لیے ٹیبل چاہیے
table_for_two.roman: Do logon ke liye table chahiye
table_for_two.note: Politer: do logon ke liye table mil jaaye gi? Table is the usual word; mez (میز) is the Urdu one.

what_recommend.note: Literally 'what's good here?'. Also: aap kya mashwara dein ge? (آپ کیا مشورہ دیں گے؟)

not_spicy.note: Literally 'please don't add chilli'. Easier to get: mirch kam daaliye ga (مرچ کم ڈالیے گا), 'less chilli'.

vegetarian_food.note: Gosht often means red meat only, so add: chicken aur machhli bhi nahin (no chicken or fish either).

no_sugar.note: Tea often comes sweetened by default. Also: baghair cheeni ke (بغیر چینی کے), 'without sugar'.

im_full.note: Same for men and women. To decline more food politely: bas, shukriya (بس، شکریہ).

takeaway.note: Also: parcel kar dijiye (پارسل کر دیجیے). Works for leftovers too.

it_was_delicious.note: Also very common: maza aa gaya! (مزہ آ گیا!), 'that was great!'

keep_change.note: Shorter: baqi rakh lijiye (باقی رکھ لیجیے).

stomach.note: Stomach ache: pet mein dard (پیٹ میں درد).

head_hurts.note: A headache: sar dard (سر درد). Also: mera sar dukh raha hai (میرا سر دکھ رہا ہے).

medicine.note: Also very common in speech: dawai (دوائی).

call_ambulance.note: In a real emergency: jaldi ambulance bulao! Numbers in Pakistan: 1122 (Rescue), 115 (Edhi).

need_rest.note: Also: mujhe aaraam karna hai (مجھے آرام کرنا ہے).

feel_better.note: Same for men and women. Also: ab main behtar hoon (اب میں بہتر ہوں).

get_well.text: اللہ آپ کو جلد شفا دے!
get_well.roman: Allah aap ko jald shifa de!
get_well.note: The usual wish. Without religious wording: jaldi theek ho jaaiye! (جلدی ٹھیک ہو جائیے!)

lets_meet.note: Literally 'let's meet sometime'. To fix a day: kal milte hain (کل ملتے ہیں), 'let's meet tomorrow'.

are_you_free.note: Same for men and women. Casual: kal free ho? (کل فری ہو؟)

call_me.note: Kijiye ga is a gentle 'please do'. Casual: mujhe call karna (مجھے کال کرنا).

your_number.text: آپ کا فون نمبر کیا ہے؟
your_number.roman: Aap ka phone number kya hai?
your_number.note: Also common: apna number de dijiye (اپنا نمبر دے دیجیے), 'please give me your number'.

see_you_soon.note: Usually followed by Allah hafiz. Also: jald mulaqaat ho gi (جلد ملاقات ہو گی).

have_nice_day.note: A modern phrase; in person people often just say Allah hafiz.

good_luck.note: Said before an exam, interview or new venture. Casual: best of luck!

thanks_a_lot.note: Even warmer: bohat bohat shukriya. Also: aap ki meharbani (آپ کی مہربانی), 'very kind of you'.

miss_you.note: Same for men and women. To an elder: mujhe aap ki yaad aati hai (مجھے آپ کی یاد آتی ہے).
